newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Chirac says Hungary can be in EU by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Chirac says Hungary can be in EU by 2000.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, beginning a two-day state visit to Budapest on Thursday, called 2000 a target date for Hungary's accession to the European Union, saying that the process was matter of "political will".

"I want your country to join the European Union in the year 2000 -- France will do everything to ensure that date is respected," he told a gathering in parliament of Hungarian legislators, officials and dignatories.

Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn said last month he hoped his country's EU membership could be achieved by the end of 2000 but EU experts have termed such a deadline unrealistic, adding that it would probably take at least two more years for the first formerly communist Central European states to join.
To warm applause, Chirac said such a target date was achievable if everyone "made the necessary efforts".
"Certain people say "it's too soon, we won't make it' -- that is to forget the years you have waited," he said. "It is also to forget that a timetable is above all a question of political will."
Negotiations with applicant states are scheduled to begin a few months after the EU's Inter-government Conference (IGC) on internal EU reform has completed its work in June this year.
Chirac proposed setting up a European conference to bring together the 15 EU members and the 11 applicant countries.
"This is not to replace accession talks but to offer every country a forum of exchange on economic, social, political and cultural issues," he said.
The French president also expressed his "unqualified support" for Hungary's application to join NATO, which he described as a historic opportunity to "bring together the European family".

Chirac's visit to Hungary is the first by a French head of state since the end of communism. Chirac's predecessor, Francois Mitterand, visited Budapest just months before Hungary held its first democratic elections in 1990.

A dozen top industrialists are accompanying the president, including the chairmen of state electricity and gas companies EDF and GDF, missiles and electronics firm Matra, construction giant Bouygues and utilities company Lyonnaise des Eaux.

Later on Thursday Chirac will address a 2,000-strong gathering of French-speaking Hungarian youth and will decorate a dozen Hungarians with French connections who distinguished themselves in the 1956 anti-Stalinist uprising.
